title: Light-Gated Ion Channels and the Optogenetic Revolution: Mechanism, Engineering and Application
content: Light-gated ion channels are retinal-binding membrane proteins that convert photons into ionic currents within milliseconds. Discovered as photoreceptors that steer algal swimming, channelrhodopsins now underpin optogenetics, in which genetically targeted expression and patterned illumination give cell-type-specific, temporally precise control over excitable and non-excitable cells. Over the past decade, sequence mining has revealed hundreds of natural variants, including anion-selective and potassium-selective channels whose conduction mechanisms evolved independently of those of cation channels. High-resolution structures and time-resolved spectroscopy are explaining how retinal isomerization is coupled to pore opening, and protein engineering has tuned selectivity, color, kinetics and light sensitivity across the visible spectrum. These tools have transformed circuit neuroscience, are being developed for cardiac rhythm control, hearing, vision and muscle, and have begun to dissect ion signaling in plants. The Nobel Prize in Physiology or Medicine 2026 was awarded jointly to Karl Deisseroth, Peter Hegemann and Georg Nagel "for their discoveries concerning light-gated ion channels and optogenetics." Here, we explain how these channels work, how they have been re-engineered and how they are now used, from neural circuits to the heart and the plant leaf.
